the rational ideologies of control, which are dominant in healthcare organisations, are detrimental to the implementation of policy for public involvement in service development.

the influence of managerial ideologies in relation to the translation of policy into practice.
how policy implementation for PI is affected by managerial ideologies of control and how this can be improved.
the continued managerial dominance over PI and its implications for the future of public involvement in healthcare decision making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NHS has not moved from a rational to normative ideology of control over PI, and therefore, the current policy emphasis on PI will remain largely peripheral to service development.
whilst the NHS has made progress in the implementation of PI, it has not gone far enough.
the influence of managerial ideologies on PI is a significant factor in the continued dominance of the status quo in healthcare policy implementation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PI can be successfully realised when organisative managers enact normative rather than rational ideologies of control.
whilst the NHS is a complex organisation, it is also a political one.
PI is more likely to be realised in the case of a normative ideology of control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
whilst PI may be alluded to in healthcare policy, it is often the case that managers are able to exert control over the extent to which it is realised in practice.
whilst PI can be successfully implemented in the NHS, the managerial dominance of the normative ideologies of managerial control can limit the scope of the PI that is enacted.
